intro: The Adagietto, the fourth movement of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony, is marked Sehr langsam and is scored for strings and harp without the symphony’s winds and brass. The strings play a melody in F major over harp notes, and the movement ends quietly and leads straight into the finale.

sections.label: A · Violin theme over harp, F major
sections.mNote: Long F major violin phrases over plucked harp notes.

sections.label: B · G-string melody, turn to G♭ major
sections.mNote: A melody on the G string; the harmony turns towards G♭ major.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns, harp and strings
sections.mNote: The strings slow as the opening theme returns.

sections.label: A″ · Violins in high register, broadening
sections.mNote: High violin notes above rising cellos and harp.

sections.label: Coda · Strings close in F major
sections.mNote: The harp stops before the final chord.

relations.label: The opening song returns
relations.basis: The Adagietto’s A–B–A′ outline restores the F-major opening after the contrasting middle span. The later excerpt lies just after the return marked near 415 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.933, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 413 s (cache/form/mahler-5-adagietto.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening bars, violas and harp
cues.text: The divided violas hold a chord while the harp begins to move. The cellos enter, then the first violins play the long melody, which Mahler marked seelenvoll, soulful.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 178, opening bars: divided violas, harp pickup, cello entry and violin melody marked seelenvoll. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/04/IMSLP13083-Mahler-Symphony_No.5_IV.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harp as continuo
cues.text: The harp takes the role of a basso continuo under the strings. Mahler left out the winds, brass and percussion used in the surrounding movements, and the Adagietto is scored for strings and harp only.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement describes the yearning tune with the harp in the role of a basso continuo: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/ . Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 178–182: the page carries staves for harp and strings only. Peter Laki’s note for the Hungarian Philharmonic: the Adagietto is scored for strings and harp only: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/v-cisz-moll-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mengelberg’s annotation on Alma
cues.text: Willem Mengelberg wrote in his score that the Adagietto was Mahler’s declaration of love to Alma, and that both Mahlers had told him so. According to his account, Mahler sent her the manuscript without a covering letter, and she understood.
cues.evidence: Mengelberg’s score annotation (“Statt eines Briefes sandte er ihr dieses im Manuskript: weiter kein Wort dazu. Sie hat es verstanden … Beide haben mir dies erzählt. WM”), quoted at https://www.alma-mahler.com/archiv_semmering_deutsch/presscorner/alma_und_musik.html and, in part, by K. Dawn Grapes: https://fcsymphony.org/mahler-adagietto/ . This is Mengelberg’s account of the manuscript’s meaning; the annotation’s date is not supplied there.

cues.title: Poem with the manuscript
cues.text: Another version of the story comes from a letter Alma wrote to Mengelberg. In it she said that Mahler had left a small poem with the manuscript: “How much I love you, you my sun, I cannot tell you in words. I can only lament to you my longing and my love.”
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement reports the poem “Wie ich dich liebe, Du meine Sonne, ich kann mit Worten Dir’s nicht sagen. Nur meine Sehnsucht kann ich Dir klagen und meine Liebe”, according to a letter Alma wrote to Mengelberg: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/ . Translation by the site.

cues.title: Middle section, violins on the G string
cues.text: At rehearsal 2 (bar 38) the tempo becomes more flowing. The first violins play on the G string, with warmth and a full tone, and the harp rests. Harp arpeggios return briefly in bars 44–46, and the string melody moves towards G♭ major, whose key signature begins at bar 47.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 180, Fliessender at rehearsal 2 (bar 38): violin G-Saite, mit Wärme, grosser Ton; brief harp return in bars 44–46, immediately before the G♭-major key signature at bar 47.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle section in G♭ major
cues.text: After a climax marked Etwas drängend the key signature changes to six flats, G♭ major, and the dynamic drops to pp subito. The harp is silent. Mahler took the second theme of the finale from this passage.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 180: Etwas drängend, a climax, then six flats and pp subito, with no harp staff on the last system. The Mahler Foundation’s movement page places the finale’s accessory theme in the middle part, where the harp is missing: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/ . Laki: one of the rondo’s episodes is derived from the Adagietto: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/v-cisz-moll-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: The strings slow and die away. Harp triplets return under held chords, and the opening melody begins again at Tempo I.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 181, rehearsal 3 and Tempo I (Molto Adagio): morendo strings, returning harp triplets and the opening melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kennedy funeral, 1968; Visconti film, 1971
cues.text: On 8 June 1968 Leonard Bernstein conducted the Adagietto at Robert Kennedy’s funeral in St Patrick’s Cathedral, New York. Three years later Luchino Visconti made it the musical centre of Death in Venice.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s performance at St Patrick’s Cathedral, 8 June 1968, and Visconti’s 1971 film: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/

cues.title: Performance timings of the Adagietto
cues.text: Mahler and Mengelberg played the Adagietto in about seven minutes. Some modern conductors take nearly twelve, and this recording lasts a little over ten. The score marks it sehr langsam, very slow.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page gives about seven minutes for Mahler and Mengelberg and nearly twelve for some modern recordings: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/ . Basinger gives seven to nine minutes for Mahler’s own performances: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/

cues.title: Final climax, violins and cellos
cues.text: The violins climb and hold their high notes while the cellos rise beneath them. Mahler marks broad bow strokes, frequent bow changes and a full tone. At the highest point the phrase slows further, marked Sehr zurückhaltend, and descends.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182: breiter Strich, viel Bogen wechseln, viel Ton and Sehr zurückhaltend around the final climax.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quotation from Mahler’s song
cues.text: The closing pages draw on Mahler’s own song Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen, “I am lost to the world”. The movement ends with its melody for “In meinem Lieben, in meinem Lied” (in my love, in my song).
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik’s Universal Edition introduction to the song says its motivic material dominates the closing complex of the Adagietto: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596 . Bettie Jo Basinger identifies the melody of “In meinem Lieben, in meinem Lied” at the close of the movement: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Close in F major, attacca
cues.text: The harp has stopped, and the strings descend to F major. Mahler marks the last chord with fermatas and “lang”, then asks for the finale to follow without a break.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final bars: harp rests after the last fortissimo chord, strings descend to F major, fermatas marked lang and attacca Rondo-Finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Harp stops; first violins at Fliessender
transitions.from: A · Violin theme over harp, F major
transitions.to: B · G-string melody, turn to G♭ major
transitions.how: The harp stops after the opening phrases. At Fliessender (rehearsal 2), the first violins begin a more mobile line, marked to be played on the G string. The harmony moves towards G♭ major. The harp returns briefly in bars 44–46, before the new key is established.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 180: rehearsal 2, violin G-Saite instruction and harp return in bars 44–46.

transitions.title: Harp triplets lead back to Tempo I
transitions.from: B · G-string melody, turn to G♭ major
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme returns, harp and strings
transitions.how: The string figures of the middle section slow through zurückhaltend and morendo. The harp re-enters in triplets under sustained string chords. At Tempo I (Molto Adagio) the opening melody returns, with plucked bass notes underneath.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 181, end of the middle section, rehearsal 3 and Tempo I.

transitions.title: Rising cellos and arco basses
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme returns, harp and strings
transitions.to: A″ · Violins in high register, broadening
transitions.how: From Noch langsamer, the cellos rise over harp arpeggios into the violins’ high phrase. Mahler marks the strings breiter Strich (broad bow strokes) as they crescendo. The basses change from pizzicato to arco under the harmony, and the final climax follows.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, Noch langsamer onwards: rising cellos, breiter Strich, crescendo and arco basses before the final climax.

transitions.title: Strings close without the harp
transitions.from: A″ · Violins in high register, broadening
transitions.to: Coda · Strings close in F major
transitions.how: The harp plays its last broad chord and then rests. Marked Sehr zurückhaltend, the strings descend and diminish through the closing harmony into F major. The final fermata is marked long, and attacca Rondo-Finale is written beneath the basses.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final system: harp rests, string diminuendo, long fermatas and attacca instruction.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, IV. Adagietto, full score (Peters, plate 9015)
source.locator: Peters score, pp. 178–182: strings and harp; the harp rests through most of the middle, returning briefly in bars 44–46.

timeline.note: Harp arpeggios play beneath sustained divided violas; cellos enter before the violin melody.
First violins play the melody above harp arpeggios, divided inner strings and pizzicato basses.
First violins rest while violas and cellos continue the phrase beneath the harp.
The high melody returns; second violins and violas sustain the inner harmony.
Both violin sections broaden the rising phrase while the harp plays arpeggios across several registers.
Second violins play the line while first violins stop; harp and lower strings continue.
The more flowing middle begins with strings alone; first violins play warmly on the G string.
The harp returns briefly during the crescendo in the middle section, playing widely spaced rising figures.
The harp stops again; divided strings play the middle section.
Harp arpeggios return to the opening texture beneath the returning violin phrase.
The violins play high and the cellos rise, above divided inner strings and harp.
The harp stops; the strings descend to the final F-major chord.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
